transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-22
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Nina Patel (AE), Marco Liu (SE), David Park (Solutions Eng); Sarah Gomez (Head of ML), Priya Desai (Platform Eng), Ethan Cole (SRE), Ravi Menon (PM)

[00:00] Nina (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Sarah: Hi Sarah here.
[00:08] Priya: Priya, on platform.
[00:10] Ethan: Ethan, SRE.
[00:12] Ravi: Ravi here.
[00:14] Marco (SE): Marco from Redwood.
[00:16] David: David on solutions.
[00:20] Nina: Awesome. Agenda — quick recap of last week's POC results, dig into TTFT and streaming, kernel choices and sequence length, then define next steps.

[02:05] Marco: Alright so I pulled the 10k-run logs you shared last week — thanks Priya — and the headline is TTFT is mostly dominated by two things for your workload: 1) model cold-start off kv cache when sequence prefix changes, and 2) the streaming buffer flush frequency.
[02:28] Sarah: When you say kv cache, you mean like KV for the attention cache? We call it k-v cache but sometimes in our notes it's k-v cash haha.
[02:34] Marco: Yeah, KV as in key-value cache. The issue we saw is that you have a lot of short prompts mixed with some 2k token long ones — so the runtime can't always reuse the same cache and we evict more often.

[04:00] Priya: To confirm, our histograms show 70% of requests under 256 tokens, 20% around 512-1k, and 10% long tail >1500. That long tail is from batch-export jobs.
[04:17] Marco: That distribution explains a lot. For TTFT the short ones should be fine, but the long ones increase mem usage and force different kernel paths.

[06:12] David: Quick note on kernel choice — we're seeing better p50 and p90 when we use the fused attention kernels on the A100-like instances vs generic fallback kernels. But the fused path is sensitive to sequence length alignment.
[06:30] Ethan: We are on GCP right now, using T4s in dev, but plan to try A100 equivalent in prod. Is Redwood recommending Dedicated for that?
[06:44] Nina: For predictable throughput and to get the fused kernels consistently, Dedicated pool helps — we can pin instance types. Hosted can do it too but you'd see more variance and potential fallback to generic kernels.

[08:01] Marco: Also streaming cadence matters. You currently flush every 128 tokens which gives steady output but TTFT goes up because of batching windows. For interactive short prompts, a flush at 32 tokens or event-driven flush can cut TTFT substantially.
[08:22] Sarah: Hmm we've been conservative to keep throughput high. But users complain about the first token lag.
[08:29] Priya: Any tradeoff on cost if we flush more often?
[08:32] Marco: Slight increase in GPU scheduling overhead — a few percent. But if you combine smaller flush with prefix caching and request-level routing (send short prompts to a low-latency pool), net cost can be neutral or even cheaper because you avoid long tail slow requests blocking batching.

[10:45] Ravi: We also wanted to understand the impact of tokenization and padding. Our preprocessing pads to 1024 for batches currently to simplify pipeline. Could that be killing us?
[10:58] Marco: Yes, padding to the max is costly; for streaming and TTFT you should bucket by length or use dynamic batching. For example, small prompts to a streaming-optimized route with dynamic batching at 32-64 tokens.

[13:20] Priya: Marco, you mentioned kernel selection is sequence-length-sensitive. Can you explain what you measured?
[13:25] Marco: Sure; on our test runs, fused kernels (we call them fused-attn) outperform generic kernels for seq lengths up to 1024, but when you get odd lengths or >1536, we fall back to a slower codepath. In your mixed distribution the scheduler sometimes picks the fallback which raises p99. We suggest trimming prompts where possible and also padding to multiples that match the fused kernels supported sizes, or choose a kernel profile that favors mixed lengths.
[15:03] David: There's also a compilation cost when switching kernels; we cache compiled kernels per sequence profile but if the mix is too high you'll see compile thrash.

[16:40] Sarah: From a compliance/security perspective, we need to know if KV cache evictions touch PII in logs. Are the eviction events logged, and are they stored?
[16:52] Nina: Good question. By default Redwood's runtime keeps cache ephemeral in-GPU; eviction logs are ephemeral too unless you enable longer retention. We'll include SOC2 notes but short answer: cache contents are not persisted to disk unless you explicitly turn on debug tracing.
[17:18] Priya: Please share the exact config flags for that — we need to show it to security.
[17:23] Nina: Yep, action item on me to send SOC2 + config checklist.

[19:00] Marco: Back to numbers — p50 TTFT for short prompts on our tuned streaming path is ~22ms on A100-class with fused kernels and KV warm. p90 is ~60ms. With generic kernels or cold KV that p90 can jump to 180-250ms.
[19:24] Ethan: Those are great if we can replicate. Our dev runs on T4s show p50~60ms and p90~230ms for similar configs.

[21:10] Marco: We're going to run a targeted streaming test that mimics your mix with 70/20/10 split, 1k requests, and measure TTFT/p50/p90/p99 and also token throughput.
[21:23] Marco: We'll try two variants: 1) fuse-kernel preferred route with dedicated A100-like machine, 2) hosted fallback path with streaming flush 32 tokens.

[23:00] Priya: For the dedicated pool sizing, what's the guidance if we want to handle 200 qps with that mix?
[23:12] David: Rough back-of-envelope — on A100v4-class we get around 40-60 streaming short prompt qps per GPU depending on batch tuning. For 200 qps you'd want 4-6 GPUs with autoscale buffer. We'll send a sizing spreadsheet.

[25:30] Sarah: Any gotchas with function calling / structured outputs and streaming? We're using function calls for enrichment and the model emits JSON sometimes across several chunks.
[25:45] Marco: Streaming and function calling work but you want to enable structured output mode and use checkpoint markers, otherwise streaming chunk boundaries can split JSON tokens and client-side parsing becomes harder. We'll share recommended client-side decoding snippets.

[28:10] Ethan: On the benchmark side, what's the best way for us to run this without exposing sensitive data? We can synthesize payloads but need similar token distributions.
[28:22] Marco: Exactly — synth payloads with same length histogram and prompt templates are perfect. If you can strip PII but keep structural tokens we can run full-stack.

[30:00] Priya: We'll share a 1k-sample of sanitized prompts and the histogram by tomorrow.
[30:10] Marco: Great. After that we'll run two 1k tests and attach full logs and kernel profiles.

[33:05] Nina: Quick pause — customers often ask about fallback policies: if fused kernels are unavailable, can we automatically route to cheaper models or degrade gracefully?
[33:20] Marco: Yes, routing rules can be set to prefer low-latency variants and fall back to higher-latency ones; we can also route small prompts to a specific low-latency pool and long jobs to batch lanes.

[35:40] Ravi: Cost question — if we move to Dedicated to get consistent kernels, what's the incremental cost vs hosted?
[35:52] Nina: Dedicated has a base commitment. For your projected usage we'd show a blended cost that for steady state is lower per token and gives latency SLO. For spiky loads, you can purchase burst credits or allow limited hosted fallback. I'll send updated pricing that shows both scenarios.

[38:25] David: On the runtime side, one more tip — enable prefix/KV caching for repeated user prefixes like system messages, that'll reduce latency significantly for short prompts.
[38:38] Priya: We do have a shared system instruction that is 120 tokens long, that could be cached.
[38:45] Marco: Exactly — if the top-of-prompt is identical, cache is a huge win.

[41:10] Sarah: Any blockers you see for us to get to a pilot next week?
[41:18] Marco: No blockers. We need your histograms and sanitized payloads, and we'll run the streaming tests. Also we need to confirm whether you want a dedicated pool trial or hosted-first.

[41:30] Priya: Let's start hosted-first with routing rules and if p90/p99 isn't stable we'll flip a small dedicated pool.

[43:00] Nina: Recap / next steps — Marco will run the streaming tests and share benchmark spreadsheet + logs by Friday. Priya to share histograms and sample prompts by Thursday. Nina to send SOC2 docs and pricing. Schedule full-stack benchmark for 2027-06-30.

[44:00] Marco: I'll include kernel trace snippets and an explanation of why truncated sequences sometimes cause fallback.

[44:10] Priya: Thanks, that will help our security review too.

[46:20] Ethan: One operational note — if we do dedicated, can we get logs to our SIEM? We need audit-level events routed to our Splunk.

[46:32] Nina: Yes, we support audit log forwarding to Splunk/CloudWatch and customer-managed KMS for key management. I'll include config docs.

[48:50] Sarah: OK let's aim for the Thursday/Friday milestones. Good call.

[49:00] Nina: Thanks everyone.

[49:05] Marco: Thanks all, we'll be in touch.

[51:20] End meeting.
